author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: The Right to Disagree
subtitle: Lanternweald — sixth expansion pass
content:
I lost the vote by three hands.

The result was announced at the same table where I'd spent two weeks helping residents understand the inspection report. Eleven favored delaying any further exploration of the lower service passage until the surface system had survived another storm season. Eight supported a limited, supervised survey sooner. I was among the eight.

Maui was standing beside me when the count finished.

He stared at the raised hands as if somebody had declared the ocean illegal.

"Eleven against eight?" he muttered. "I've won harder fights with worse odds."

"This isn't a fight," I told him.

"Everything's a fight if you say it dramatically enough."

Mini Maui drew a little voting tally against his chest, then erased the losing side with both hands. Maui covered the tattoo with his palm.

"That is not how voting works," I whispered.

"I know. I just can't believe eight people can be this right and still lose. Clearly the problem is that nobody let me deliver the opening speech."

Neither did I. I'd spent weeks making a case, and it stung to find people wanted to wait. Maui wasn't going to become a gentle lecturer on parliamentary procedure because a romance demanded it. He would complain, pace, and probably compose a terrible rhyme about committees. He could still respect the result.

"Can we tell them I think they're being a little ridiculous?" he asked.

"Yes. Politely."

"You're taking all the fun out of democracy."

I laughed despite myself. He stayed while the minority concerns were read into the minutes. Every once in a while his jaw tightened, but he didn't use his hook to settle the argument.

"That's ridiculous," he whispered.

I could feel my face burn.

It wasn't ridiculous. People had listened, argued, and chosen a course I hadn't wanted.

Knowing that did not make disappointment easier.

The meeting had been difficult from the start. Avel argued that the old route should never open again because the Closed Bells history was too dangerous. Fen pointed out that a water channel did not become evil because officials misused access to it. Sela asked why any plan should proceed before the surface repairs proved they would protect her home. Tamsin warned that a tunnel under an ancient arch couldn't be treated like a gate you simply pulled off its hinges.

I had supported a narrower survey. Not reopening the barrier, not sending people into water, just funding another inspection of the dry upper approach before the next budget cycle.

The last testimony belonged to Edda.

She didn't bring a speech. She brought a scale drawing of the upper access route and placed it on the table where everyone could reach it.

"If you authorize an inspection," she said, "you need to decide how the crew gets back out when the weather changes. The ridge turns are too narrow for a loaded equipment cart, and the lower stair is still closed."

Tamsin leaned over the plan.

"We could carry the instruments by hand."

"Could you? With someone who has been injured?"

Nobody answered.

Avel looked at the map. "Then we wait."

"Or we cost a safer route," Edda replied. "I'm not voting on whether history is frightening. I'm telling you the access plan is incomplete."

Edda opened her inspection folder to a page covered in hand-drawn turning arcs. I had seen the page before. What I hadn't seen was the second tracing underneath, one with a tighter curve and an old set of measurements crossed out in red.

"That was the first design," she said. "I tested it with a loaded handcart and with someone who uses a mobility aid. Neither could make the return turn without backing into the work area. If the passage were open, we would have no usable emergency exit."

Maui frowned. "I could carry a cart."

"You could," Edda answered. "What happens when you're at sea?"

"Then I'd come back."

"And while you're coming back?"

He looked at the plans. I could almost see him searching for a victory large enough to make the measurements stop mattering.

I had argued for the survey because I wanted us to know what lay behind the old closure. I still did. But the drawing in my hand told me the eight votes I'd counted hadn't solved the question of who could leave an unsafe site.

"Could we ask the people who use the upper path to test a new route first?" I said.

"Yes," Edda replied. "With their permission, with the work hours funded, and without pretending that a successful surface test opens the sealed lower passage."

Maui tilted his head. "You mean the enormous, magnificent me is not the emergency plan?"

"Correct."

"Terrible choice. Statistically the most magnificent emergency plan in the world."

He stepped back from the table anyway. The vote hadn't become a less painful result. The people who would have to live with it had become harder to overlook.

I felt the argument I'd prepared shrink in my mouth. I'd counted the cost of the survey equipment and the time of the engineers. I hadn't counted the work of making the survey possible without treating people's bodies as interchangeable parts.

Maui glanced at me.

"You didn't know that," he whispered.

"No."

"Should we say something?"

"Yes."

When the chair invited final responses, I admitted the gap in my proposal and asked that the access estimate become part of the public record, whether the survey passed or not. Fen supported the amendment. Avel supported it too.

For one uncomfortable moment, I was relieved that people who disagreed with me were helping fix something I'd missed.

The amended motion was recorded before the final vote. No one clapped. The decision mattered more for what it authorized than for how anyone felt about it.

The council chose to wait.

I sat through the closing remarks with my notebook open and nothing written on the page.

Outside, Maui followed me toward the fountain.

"They wouldn't listen."

"They did listen."

"Then why did they vote against you?"

"Because they disagreed."

He looked at me as though I'd insulted the entire idea of argument.

I stopped by the railing.

"Maui, I don't like the result either. But I won't call it unfair because it didn't go my way."

"Some of them were frightened."

"That doesn't invalidate their vote."

"Fear doesn't build bridges."

"Sometimes it stops people from walking onto one that isn't ready."

He turned away, jaw tight.

I let him go a few paces.

Then I followed.

We found Fen near the market, putting the final survey notes into a folder. They looked exhausted.

"Happy?" Maui asked.

Fen raised an eyebrow.

"With the decision?"

"Yes."

"No. I'd have preferred a funded survey. But I understand why the majority wants to see the surface channel tested first."

Maui frowned.

"Then why aren't you angry?"

"I am," Fen said. "I can be angry and still respect a process."

That stopped him.

Fen tucked the folder under their arm.

"If you want to help, bring the next tide measurements on time. We still have work to do."

Maui watched them leave.

For a moment he looked younger than I'd ever seen him, not in his face but in the way a person can be caught between what they want and what the world will allow.

"I thought if we explained it well enough, they'd agree," he said.

"So did I."

"And now?"

"Now we do the work that was approved, keep collecting evidence, and bring the question back when we have new information."

He sighed.

"You're very annoying when you're reasonable."

"I've been told."

We walked to the sea-glass garden, where the plants had grown tall enough to cast narrow shadows across the path. Ilya was checking the bench's armrests. I asked whether they wanted a hand.

"No thanks," they said. "I've got it."

We sat on the next bench.

I took out my notebook and finally wrote down the result. Under it I listed the concerns raised by the majority: uncertainty about old mortar, cost of additional testing, emergency evacuation access, and fear of repeating a historic wrong.

Then I wrote the reasons I still disagreed.

Maui watched.

"Why both?"

"Because if we only keep the arguments that won, we forget what was at stake for everyone else."

He considered that.

"Can I add something?"

I handed him the pencil.

He wrote: *People are afraid of being trapped again.*

Then below it, after a moment: *People are also afraid of being flooded again.*

I looked at him.

"That's good."

"Don't sound so surprised."

I smiled.

By evening the square had quieted. The council's notice remained posted. Nobody had been banished for dissent. Nobody's name was written beside a declaration of disloyalty. The paths remained open to travelers who wanted to leave, while the unsafe maintenance passage stayed sealed.

The vote had not solved the old wrong.

It had decided what we would do next.

At home, Maui cooked dinner while I wrote a message to Neri confirming that the minority's concerns should be included in the minutes. He burned the first piece of bread, apologized to no one in particular, and tried again.

After supper he stood beside me at the window.

"Are you still angry?"

"Yes."

"Want me to make a speech about it?"

"Absolutely not."

He laughed.

I rested my head against his shoulder.

"Will you come to the next meeting?" I asked.

"Yes."

"Even if we lose again?"

He thought about it.

"Yes."

That answer mattered more than a victory.

Fen laid our notes beside the previous week's marks.

"The surface channel is holding," they said. "Not perfectly. There's a small area collecting silt, and the planting bed on the south bank still needs watching."

"Does that change the council vote?" Maui asked.

"No. The vote was about when to survey the old lower service passage. Today's data tells us how the approved surface repairs are behaving."

He sighed.

"You're going to keep saying that."

"Until it stops being necessary."

Fen handed me the pencil and asked me to mark the silt line on the public chart. I did, careful not to draw the channel as safer than it was. A person planning a walk along the ridge needed the actual conditions, not our disappointment with the council.

Later, Neri sent word that the minutes included both our objections and Edda's access estimate. The record hadn't rewritten the vote. It had simply made the disagreement available to anyone willing to read it.

Maui looked at the note.

"Does this count as winning something?"

"Maybe the right to try again with better evidence."

He considered.

"Very small victory."

"Some of the best ones are."

We went to help Fen clean the tide board, which was considerably less glamorous than a council chamber and considerably more useful that morning.

The next morning we took the tide measurements to Fen, exactly when we had promised.

The sea hadn't voted.

It still needed tending.
